6. Triplet Loss Introduced
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446563560-987206054.png

This connects back to recapping Siamese networks, already covered in this topic. Triplet loss genuinely compares three examples at once: an anchor, a genuinely similar positive, and a genuinely different negative.
Training genuinely pushes the anchor-positive distance below the anchor-negative distance by some genuine margin, the exact core training signal explored throughout the rest of this topic.

10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates computing triplet loss, already covered in this topic, for an anchor, positive, and negative example.

code.content:
import math

def euclidean_distance(a, b):
    # already covered as a distance in the embedding space in this topic
    return math.sqrt(sum((x - y) ** 2 for x, y in zip(a, b)))

anchor = [0.5, 0.6, 0.1]      # already covered as the anchor example in this topic
positive = [0.55, 0.58, 0.12]  # already covered as a genuinely similar example in this topic
negative = [0.1, 0.9, 0.8]     # already covered as a genuinely different example in this topic

def triplet_loss(anchor, positive, negative, margin=0.2):
    # already covered as triplet loss introduced in this topic
    pos_distance = euclidean_distance(anchor, positive)
    neg_distance = euclidean_distance(anchor, negative)
    return max(0, pos_distance - neg_distance + margin)

pos_dist = euclidean_distance(anchor, positive)
neg_dist = euclidean_distance(anchor, negative)
print(f"Anchor-positive distance (already covered in this topic): {pos_dist:.3f}")
print(f"Anchor-negative distance: {neg_dist:.3f}")

loss = triplet_loss(anchor, positive, negative)
print(f"\nTriplet loss (already covered in this topic): {loss:.4f}")
print("A loss of zero genuinely means the margin requirement is already genuinely satisfied")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows a low or zero triplet loss when the anchor sits genuinely much closer to the positive than to the negative, exactly the margin-based separation already covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Metric learning trains a model whose entire job is producing useful distances between examples.
It makes distance itself the direct, explicit target of training, building on embedding spaces used throughout this course.
A good learned metric places truly similar examples close and truly different examples far.
Metric learning commonly reuses the Siamese network structure, comparing examples through one shared encoder.
Triplet loss compares an anchor, a positive, and a negative, enforcing a margin between distances.
Contrastive loss compares pairs at a time; triplet loss compares three examples together.
A well trained metric lets new classes be recognized from just a few examples.
Metric learning suits tasks needing meaningful similarity; standard classification suits fixed categories.
Next up: Few-Shot Learning, building directly on this metric-based recognition capability.
